https://www.dw.com/en/zimbabwe-crash-inv.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Jchy The accident occurred on Friday about 87 miles south of the capital Harare [FILE: April 20, 2020] Image: Zinyange Auntony/AFP Advertisement At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured. Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare. The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement. Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell. Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed. Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor. In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa. Rescue personnel work at the site of a bus accident on a major highway near Harare [FILE: January 18, 2015] Image: Xinhua/imago images Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate , the commission says. This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet. https://www.indcatholicnews.com/news/559.text: Home News UK & Ireland US & Canada World Obituaries & Tributes Justice, Peace & Environment Education Youth & Young Adults Reflections Reflections & Homilies Viewpoint Letters Blogs Arts & Culture Gospel in Art Art, Theatre, Music & Shows Films, TV & Radio Books Poetry Travel Listings Forthcoming Events Regular Events Classified Ads Jobs Courses & Voluntary Work Retreat, Spirituality and Pilgrimage Centres Businesses, Accommodation & Travel Prayers Contact Resources Links About Martyrs of Pratulin by Walery Eljasz Radzikowski Source: Vatican Media During the General Audience on Wednesday, Pope Leo XIV recalled the Polish martyrs of Pratulin: Blessed Wincenty Lewoniuk and his Twelve Companions. The Greek Catholics were killed by soldiers of the Russian Empire in the 19th century after refusing to abandon their faith. "Thirty years ago, Saint John Paul II beatified Wincenty Lewoniuk and his Twelve Companions, martyrs who defended, to the point of shedding their blood, their belonging to the Catholic Church and their unity with the Successor of Saint Peter, while remaining faithful to their own Eastern tradition," Pope Leo XIV said in his greeting to Polish pilgrims during the General Audience. "I entrust to their intercession the cause of unity among Christ's disciples and Catholics who are persecuted today for their faith," the Pope added. The Greek Catholic Church emerged in the territories of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth following the Union of Brest in 1596. Its members came to be known as 'Uniates.' Part of the Orthodox hierarchy and faithful recognised the authority of the Pope and embraced the Catholic faith while retaining the Eastern rite. In the 19th century, the Uniates - Greek Catholics living in eastern Poland, which at the time was under Russian rule - were pressured by the Tsarist authorities to join the Orthodox Church. Those who refused to renounce communion with the Catholic Church faced persecution. Some were killed, while others were deported to Siberia. Wincenty Lewoniuk and his Twelve Companions were lay Catholics belonging to the Uniate Church. Most were farmers from villages in the Podlasie region - husbands, fathers, and young men united by deep faith and attachment to the Catholic Church and their Eastern tradition. On 24 January 1874, they gathered to defend their Uniate church in Pratulin, in what is now eastern Poland. The commander of the Russian troops ordered his soldiers to open fire on the unarmed men as they knelt in the snow. The Martyrs of Pratulin came to symbolize fidelity to the Catholic faith and the unity of the Church under the leadership of the Successor of Peter, making their witness a clear call to unity. Pope Pius XII recalled the inhabitants of Pratulin in his Encyclical Orientales omnes Ecclesias, issued to mark the 350th anniversary of the Union of Brest. He referred to the tragic circumstances in which they defended their church from being converted into an Orthodox place of worship. He expressed the hope that one day they might be venerated among the blessed in heaven. Pope Leo XIV's words echo the message of Saint John Paul II during the Beatification Mass celebrated at the Vatican 30 years ago, on 6 October 1996, as the Church marked the 400th anniversary of the Union of Brest. Speaking on that occasion, Pope John Paul II said that Wincenty Lewoniuk and his Twelve Companions, raised that day to the honours of the altars, "through their example and intercession, invite us all to continue courageously on the path towards the full unity of the entire family of Christ's disciples, in the spirit of the ecumenical teaching of the Second Vatican Council."
